ghost.sample:
Zog was a small dragon. He lived behind the moon. He loved to eat clouds.  
One day, Zog saw a big cloud. It was gray and soft. He wanted it.  
But the cloud was high up. Zog could not reach it. He felt sad.  
Then he saw a little kite. It went up and up.  
Zog smiled. He flew next to the kite. The kite helped him get high.  
At last, Zog ate the cloud. It was fluffy and nice.  
He felt happy and full.  
Then he saw more clouds. He looked at them and laughed.  
He went back behind the moon and was asleep in his cozy place.  
The moon gave light. Zog was warm and safe. He dreamed of clouds.

Zog was a small dragon, and Zog lived behind the moon. Zog ate clouds when he was hungry. He liked fluffy clouds best. One day, Zog looked out and saw one tiny cloud far away. It was white and soft. Zog wanted it. But the cloud was high up. Zog could not reach it. He felt sad. Then a bird flew by. The bird said, "I can help." The bird flew up and brought the cloud down. Zog ate it and smiled. He was very happy. He shared a small cloud with the bird too. They sat behind the moon and looked at the sky. Zog felt warm and safe. Then he was asleep next to the moon and dreamed of more clouds.

Sisi was a little cloud. Sisi lives in the sky. Sisi likes to sing songs.  
One day, Sisi saw a bird in the sky. The bird looked sad.  
"Why are you sad?" asked Sisi.  
The bird said, "I lost my song."  
Sisi thought hard. Then Sisi sang a soft song.  
The bird listened. Then he smiled.  
"I remember it now!" said the bird.  
He sang with Sisi. Their songs were small and sweet.  
Soon the sky felt bright and kind.  
The bird flew near and said, "Thank you, Sisi."  
Sisi smiled and sang again. The bird sang too.  
They played in the sky until the sun went down.  
Sisi felt happy. The bird felt happy too.  
It was a very nice day in the sky.

Sisi was a little cloud. Sisi lives in the sky. Sisi likes to sing songs.  
One day, Sisi saw Timmy in the park. Timmy had a red ball.  
He wanted to play, but the ball went under a big bush.  
"Oh no," said Timmy. "I can not get it."  
Sisi looked down from the sky. Sisi sang a song.  
The song was soft and sweet.  
The wind moved the bush a little. Then the ball rolled out.  
Timmy smiled big. "Thank you, Sisi!" he said.  
He threw the ball up and down.  
Sisi laughed. "You are fun," said Sisi.  
Timmy played with the ball for a long time.  
Sisi stayed in the sky and sang songs while Timmy played.  
At the end, Timmy waved up high.  
Sisi waved back and sang a happy song. The day felt nice.

Pip was a tiny robot. Pip lived in a little house near a park. Pip loved red apples. Pip had a red apple on a plate. Pip smiled at it all day. But then the wind blew hard. The apple rolled away. Pip looked and looked. He went under a bench. He went by a tree. Then he saw the red apple in some grass. Pip was so happy. A girl named Mia was there too. She said, "You found it!" Pip said, "Yes, I did!" Mia helped him carry the apple home. At home, Pip ate the red apple with a big smile. When night came, Pip slept in a teapot. He felt warm and safe. The little robot dreamed of more red apples.

Pip was a tiny robot. Pip loved red apples. Pip slept in a teapot. One day, Pip went to the park with Tom. Tom had a big red apple. Pip looked at it and smiled. Then the apple rolled away on the grass. Pip ran after it. Tom ran too. The apple went by a bench and then by a tree. Pip felt sad for a little while. Tom said, "We can find it." Pip looked under leaves. At last, Pip found the red apple by a flower. Pip picked it up with care. "Thank you," said Tom. Pip smiled. Tom gave Pip the apple to hold for a bit. Then Pip and Tom sat on the grass and ate little snacks. Later, Pip went home. Pip got into the teapot and slept. Pip was happy.

guide.question: Why do some stories get turned away?
guide.answer: Some stories get turned away because the app checks every one against fixed rules. A story must be between one hundred and one hundred eighty words, keep every sentence under twenty words, use only words the tiny mind has met often enough, and keep the character facts word for word: the name, the kind, and both special things.
problems: Mostly correct and clear, but it adds 'often enough' to the word rule. The requirement is only that the words were met in the stories it grew up on, not a frequency threshold.

guide.question: Why do some stories get turned away?
guide.answer: Stories can get turned away because they need to be between one hundred and one hundred eighty words long, with no sentence longer than twenty words. They can only use words that the tiny mind has often seen in its training, and every story must keep the character's facts exactly as they are: the name, the kind, and both special things. These are strict rules the app follows, not a judgment of quality. DO: SHOW writer.

guide.question: Why switch parts off instead of just looking at the attention?
guide.answer: Because attention only gives clues about where the model is looking, not proof of what actually causes the answer. Switching parts off is the test for causation, and the unrelated controls and name swap help show whether a part is selective for this fact or just generally active.

guide.question: Why switch parts off instead of just looking at the attention?
guide.answer: Switching parts off helps to determine if those parts are causally contributing to predicting the fact, while attention can show correlation but does not prove causation. It's like checking if a singer's voice is needed for a choir piece, rather than just looking at the notes they sing. Both approaches give valuable insights, but they answer different questions.
